sources.title: Plan 9 from Bell Labs (canonical overview essay)
The Use of Name Spaces in Plan 9
The Organization of Networks in Plan 9
bind, mount, unmount(2) — change name space

structure.rationale: The book follows the split the requester specified: Part 1 (The Plan 9 Model) lays down the three composing pillars — files as the uniform resource interface, 9P as the single protocol that reaches them, and the per-process namespace that assembles them into a program's view — using the 'Plan 9 from Bell Labs' overview paper as the grounding source, with no history or biography. Part 2 then walks outward from the same three pillars in dependency order: Namespaces (the abstraction itself) before 9P Protocol (the wire mechanism namespaces are built from) before File Servers (the things namespaces name and 9P talks to); Mount, Bind, and Union Directories follow as the operators that construct a namespace from those servers; Process Namespaces then shows how that construction interacts with rfork/process lifecycle; Plumbing is placed next as a worked example of the whole model — an ordinary file server used as an interprocess bus; and Security and the Capability Model closes the book, since Plan 9's security design (no setuid, factotum, capabilities) is best understood as a consequence of everything established before it — namespace restriction standing in for privilege. Each concept builds strictly on the ones before it, so a reader who proceeds in order never meets an unexplained mechanism.
structure.audience: Technically savvy readers already comfortable with systems programming and Unix-family OS concepts, who want Plan 9's actual design and mechanisms — not its history — explained precisely.

claims.text: Plan 9's design rests on three composing ideas: resources are named and accessed like files in a hierarchical file system; a single protocol, 9P, is used to access those resources whether they are local or remote; and the disjoint hierarchies exposed by different services are joined by the client into one private hierarchical name space.

Plan 9 applies the file/directory metaphor far more broadly than traditional Unix: windows, network connections, running processes, the mouse, the graphics device, and remote machines' resources are all represented as files or directory trees that are opened, read, written, and closed with the same small set of operations, rather than through separate special-case system calls (ioctl, socket options, and the like).

9P is the one protocol used to reach every resource in the system: the kernel speaks it to serve local devices, and the identical protocol is used over a network connection to talk to a file server on another machine, so a remote resource is reached exactly the same way as a local one.

Every process has its own private name space — its own view of the file hierarchy — rather than sharing one global file tree; a name space is assembled by binding and mounting resource trees (served locally by the kernel or remotely by a 9P server) at chosen points.

Because a name space is just a client-side composition of file trees reached over 9P, building a custom view of the system requires no new system calls or kernel support for each new kind of resource — adding a resource to your world is a bind or mount, not a new API.

The window system, 8½, is itself an ordinary file server: it serves files such as /dev/cons and /dev/bitblt, and gives each window client a distinct copy of those files in that window's own local name space, so the same path name (e.g. /dev/cons) resolves to a different underlying resource depending on whose name space is doing the resolving.

Conventional path names (such as /net, /dev, /proc, /bin) are consistent across every Plan 9 machine, but what is actually bound or mounted underneath those names — and therefore what a program actually finds there — can differ per process and per machine; a program always knows where to look, not necessarily what it will find.

Some conventional directories are union directories — a single directory backed by several component directories bound together and searched in order — used, for example, so that /bin resolves to the right set of executables for the current architecture without a program needing to know which one is active.

Network access is exposed as a file hierarchy under /net: a protocol directory (e.g. /net/tcp) contains a clone file used to reserve a new connection (reading it returns a connection number), and each numbered connection directory exposes ctl and data files — writing a connect command to ctl establishes the connection, and data carries the bytes — so dialing out is ordinary file I/O rather than a socket system call.

9P governs whole file systems, not individual files in isolation: it includes the procedures to resolve names and walk the hierarchy the server exports, and it operates at the level of bytes rather than fixed blocks — a deliberate difference from block-oriented network file protocols such as NFS. The client's assembled name space is held entirely on the client side, never on or shared with the server, which is itself a departure from name-space designs like Sprite's.

Plan 9's own overview paper frames the payoff with a naming analogy: 'my house' and a house's precise postal address name the same place, but the informal phrase is easier to say, means something only in context, and changes meaning depending on who says it — exactly how a Plan 9 path such as /dev/cons or /bin/date is a conventional, context-dependent name, while what actually answers it is local and can legitimately differ from process to process and machine to machine.

The window system 8½ demonstrates the three pillars composing into distribution transparency: each window is created with its own private name space, so a program running in a remote window still just opens /dev/mouse, /dev/bitblt, and /dev/cons as usual — it 'does not know whether the files are local,' because the 9P connection to the file server providing them is already established and multiplexed into that window's namespace before the program ever runs.

snippets.code:
open  /net/tcp/clone            -> read: connection number "n"
write /net/tcp/n/ctl  "connect 192.0.2.1!80"
write /net/tcp/n/data  ...      -> bytes sent on the connection
read  /net/tcp/n/data           -> bytes received on the connection
snippets.note: The classic /net dialing sequence, simplified from the protocol-directory description in net.html — plain opens/reads/writes on ctl and data files, no socket(2)/connect(2) call involved.

snippets.code:
; ns
bind -a /386/bin /bin
bind -a /rc/bin /bin
bind '#c' /dev
bind '#d' /fd
mount -A /srv/boot /n/other
snippets.note: Illustrative shape of `ns` output (per-process namespace listing) — bind/mount lines built from kernel devices ('#c', '#d') and mounted 9P services; exact lines vary by machine and session.

pitfalls: Readers from a Unix background tend to assume a bind or mount is a global, persistent change (like editing /etc or adding a symlink). In Plan 9 it changes only the acting process's name space (and any process that shares it) — the same bind performed in one window is invisible from another window's shell unless the name space is explicitly shared or the change is made before the fork that separated them.

"Everything is a file" in Plan 9 is easy to under-read as just Unix's version of the same slogan. Plan 9 pushes further: Unix still special-cases sockets, ioctls, and many device controls outside the ordinary file interface, whereas Plan 9 routes control operations themselves (e.g. dialing a network connection, above) through plain opens/reads/writes on ctl and data files, which is what lets one protocol (9P) and one client interface cover them all.

The three pillars are easy to state as a checklist and easy to under-appreciate as a system: the payoff is specifically that they compose — file-naming (pillar 1) is what makes one protocol sufficient (pillar 2), and one protocol is what makes client-side name-space assembly (pillar 3) possible without kernel changes for every new resource type. Explaining any one pillar in isolation, without the composition, misses the actual design contribution.

A 'uniform global name space' is not the same claim as Plan 9's design, and conflating them is a common misreading. Plan 9 explicitly does not give everyone the same tree; it gives everyone the same conventional path names (/dev/cons, /bin/date, /net) resolved against a locally assembled namespace, so the guarantee is 'a program always knows where to look,' not 'every machine sees identical contents there.'

claims.text: A name space is a per-process attribute: a single rooted hierarchy of file names, assembled by binding and mounting service trees at chosen points. Unlike a conventional kernel's one global, shared file tree, Plan 9 has no such tree at all — every process's view is its own, and the file server itself never sees or holds the assembled result, only its own local hierarchy.

bind(char *name, char *old, int flag) grafts a file or directory already visible somewhere in the current name space onto another point (old) in that same name space. It requires no server communication and no open connection — it only rearranges names already reachable. The evaluation of name happens at bind time, not on each later lookup through old, so a later change to what name resolves to does not retroactively change old.

mount(int fd, int afd, char *old, int flag, char *aname) attaches the entire file tree served over an already-open, already-connected file descriptor fd (a pipe or network connection to a 9P server) so that its root appears at old. A kernel file-system type called the mount device is the sole bridge between the ordinary procedural interface user code sees (open/read/write/close) and the RPC messages that actually cross the wire to the server — the mount device does the marshaling and multiplexing, and it's the only integral RPC mechanism in Plan 9.

Both bind and mount take a flag governing how new content joins whatever is already at old: the default (MREPL) replaces old outright; MBEFORE/MAFTER instead add the new directory to the front or back of a union directory, searched in that order; MCREATE additionally marks a unioned directory as eligible to receive files a later create places there. (The full mechanics of union lookup, creation, and unmount are covered in the next chapter, Mount, Bind, and Union Directories — this chapter only needs that the two operators exist and what they attach.)

A name space's propagation across process creation is controlled explicitly, not implied by a single fork() semantics: plain fork() (equivalent to rfork(RFFDG|RFREND|RFPROC)) shares the parent's name space with the child — they become two processes pointing at one name space object, so a bind or mount performed by either is immediately visible to the other. rfork(RFNAMEG) instead gives the child a private copy, identical at the instant of the call but independent thereafter. rfork(RFCNAMEG) gives the child a wholly empty name space that must be built from nothing by mounting an open file descriptor onto it (RFNAMEG and RFCNAMEG are mutually exclusive).

Because a shared name space is literally one object referenced by multiple processes rather than copies kept in sync, the precise term for a set of processes sharing a name space this way is a name-space group — bind(2)/mount(2)'s own description defines their scope as 'the current process and other processes in its name space group.' RFNOMNT additionally can be set on a new name space to forbid further mounts and dereferencing of kernel-device names beginning with '#' inside it — useful for building a deliberately restricted namespace (relevant later for the security model).

A Plan 9 process's name space is not built from an empty root by hand each time: init(8) constructs the initial one from a namespace(6) description file, interpreted by the newns/addns library routines. Each line is one operation — mount, bind, import, cd, unmount, clear (rfork(RFCNAMEG), i.e. start over empty), or '.  path' to include another such file — using the same option letters (-a/-b/-c/-C) as the bind(1)/mount(1) commands. Every later bind or mount a running process performs builds on top of that starting point; the description file is a bootstrap, not a permanent record.

ns(1) prints a live process's actual name space (by default the caller's own, or a given pid's) as a script of bind/mount/import commands that could, in principle, reconstruct it — derived by reading and reformatting /proc/pid/ns. It is the closest thing Plan 9 offers to a name-space inspector, and by default it also rewrites raw /net/tcp/N/data paths back into readable network addresses.

Name-space construction is what buys customization without new mechanism: binaries for a given CPU architecture live in an architecture-named directory (e.g. /mips/bin), and each machine binds the one it needs to the conventional name /bin; a directory of a user's private binaries is typically unioned in ahead of it. The Plan 9 shell, rc, has no PATH variable at all — the 'which directories hold runnable commands' problem that Unix solves per-shell-instance with an environment variable is instead solved once, structurally, by the name space itself.

Name-space construction is what buys transparency: the window system, 8½, is an ordinary 9P server for files such as /dev/cons, /dev/mouse, and /dev/bitblt; each window gets its own private copies of those names bound into its own name space. A client program addressing /dev/cons has no way to ask, and no need to know, whether that window (and therefore that file) is being served locally or by a machine across the network — the same mechanism plumbed through import lets Plan 9 run X11 as an ordinary 8½ client with a measured ~10% graphics performance cost over a bare local Plan 9 machine.

Name-space construction is what makes most special-case system calls disappear: process control that Unix spreads across kill(2), ptrace(2), and assorted /proc conventions is, on Plan 9, plain text I/O on files under /proc/pid — writing 'kill' or 'stop' to ctl, reading status for state, reading/writing mem for a debugger, writing note to deliver a signal-like note. The command ps is close to a reformatted cat /proc/*/status; a debugger opens /proc/pid/text and /proc/pid/mem directly, with no ptrace-equivalent call anywhere.

import host [remotepath] mountpoint extends a local name space across a network at no special-purpose cost: it dials the remote machine, starts a 9P server there for the requested subtree, calls mount to attach that connection locally, then exits — leaving the remote process to keep serving. Concrete uses from the source paper: importing a remote floppy drive (import lab.pc /a: /n/dos) and importing a remote /proc for cross-machine debugging (import helix /proc; db /proc/27/text /proc/27/mem), the latter working across CPU architectures because db reads the target's byte order from the executable header on the text file rather than assuming its own.

The cpu command builds an entirely new name space on a remote CPU server by re-importing the pieces of the terminal's local name space that the shell needs (terminal-resident devices), while CPU-local resources such as the fast local file system connection stay local — so working 'on' the CPU server feels like the local processor simply got faster, not like moving to a different login session. The paper contrasts this explicitly with rlogin, which moves the user into a wholly distinct remote name space, and with NFS, which keeps one uniform name space but forces execution to stay on the client.

snippets.note: Exact signatures from bind(2)/mount(2)/unmount(2); flag is one of MREPL, MBEFORE, MAFTER, optionally OR'd with MCREATE (mount also has MCACHE).

snippets.code:
rfork(RFFDG|RFREND|RFPROC)   // == plain fork(): shares the name space with the parent
rfork(RFNAMEG |RFPROC)       // child gets a private COPY of the parent's name space
rfork(RFCNAMEG|RFPROC)       // child starts with an EMPTY name space
snippets.note: fork(2) is literally defined as this rfork() call; RFNAMEG and RFCNAMEG are mutually exclusive.

snippets.code:
# a namespace(6) description file, interpreted by newns() at login
mount -a tcp!fileserver!564 /root
bind -a /root/386/bin /bin
bind -a /root/rc/bin  /bin
bind '#c' /dev
cd /usr/glenda
snippets.note: Illustrative shape of a namespace(6) file (mount/bind/cd operations); exact contents are site- and machine-specific.

snippets.code:
cat /proc/*/status                # a crude ps
echo stop >/proc/17/ctl           # suspend process 17 — no ptrace() call
db /proc/27/text /proc/27/mem     # attach a debugger — local or, via import, remote
snippets.note: Process control as plain file I/O under /proc, replacing kill/ptrace/wait-family special calls.

pitfalls: It's tempting to assume rfork's name-space handling defaults to 'copy,' matching how fork() behaves for memory in most systems. Plan 9's plain fork() actually SHARES the name space object outright — RFNAMEG is the flag that copies it. Forgetting this is a real source of bugs: a bind performed in what you thought was an isolated child is visible everywhere else in the same name-space group, because there was never a separate copy to isolate it.

MREPL/MBEFORE/MAFTER control where new content lands relative to what's already there; MCREATE is a separate, independently-set flag controlling where a later create places a new file within a union. Assuming 'appended with -a' also implies 'new files get created here' is wrong — that's MCREATE's job alone, and it's easy to bind something read-only into a union and be surprised when creates keep landing in a different, older element.

A namespace(6) file describes how a name space is built at login/init time, not a live, continuously-enforced policy — bind, mount, and unmount are ordinary system calls any process can call at any later moment. Most real Plan 9 customization (a shell's local rebinding for debugging, iostats wrapping a command's namespace to gather I/O statistics, cpu rebuilding a remote namespace on login) happens by processes mutating their own already-running name space long after boot, not by re-invoking init.
